overview: Auckland International Airport owns and operates New Zealand's largest and only true gateway international airport, sitting on 1,500 hectares on the Mangere peninsula and handling roughly 75% of the country's international arrivals and 66% of domestic seat capacity. The company runs a dual-till model combining Commerce Commission-monitored aeronautical charges (airfield and passenger services) with unregulated commercial operations spanning retail, car parking, and an increasingly large property and logistics portfolio. It also holds a 24.99% stake in Queenstown Airport, giving it exposure to New Zealand's key tourism gateway.

business_model.summary: Revenue is split roughly evenly between regulated/semi-regulated aeronautical income (airfield charges and passenger services charge, tied to passenger volumes and a Commerce Commission-overseen target return) and unregulated commercial income (retail concessions, car parking, and a growing rental/property book from logistics, office, retail and hotel assets). Aeronautical and retail revenue are largely transactional/volume-linked to passenger throughput; property rental income is long-duration, contracted and increasingly the more predictable growth engine as new developments are commissioned.

revenue_streams.name: Other (rates recoveries, interest income, other income)

business_model.customer_type: B2B (28 airlines, ~300 commercial tenants/retailers, logistics and office tenants) and B2C (18.7m annual passengers, car park users, hotel guests)
business_model.geographic_mix: Single-site New Zealand asset (Auckland); revenue economically linked to international visitor arrivals (Australia, US, China as top source markets) and outbound Kiwi travel, plus domestic NZ property/logistics tenants

main_competitors: Sydney Airport (competing long-haul hub for transit/stopover traffic)
Alternative NZ logistics/industrial property landlords (Goodman Property Trust, Precinct Properties, Argosy)
competitive_position.market_position: De facto monopoly gateway for international air travel into New Zealand's largest city and economic hub; handles the majority of national international passenger and cargo volumes with very high barriers to a competing greenfield international airport

moat_factors.description: Only international airport serving Auckland (37%+ of NZ population); essentially impossible to replicate given land, consenting and capital requirements, giving durable pricing power subject only to Commerce Commission oversight
1,500ha landholding, single runway plus new domestic terminal and airfield expansion under construction; multi-decade asset life with high switching costs for airlines and tenants

658,000sqm of commercial property, logistics hub, hotels and a new outlet centre (Manawa Bay) generate contracted rental income (99% occupancy) that diversifies away from pure aeronautical/passenger cyclicality
Largest catchment and connectivity in NZ attracts airline capacity allocation over smaller regional airports, reinforcing hub status

weaknesses: Regulated aeronautical pricing is subject to Commerce Commission oversight (information disclosure regime) that constrains returns and creates political/airline pushback risk
Heavily dependent on discretionary international/domestic travel demand and airline capacity decisions largely outside its control (e.g., Air New Zealand engine issues, global fuel price shocks)
Single-site concentration risk (seismic, volcanic, flooding — as experienced in the Jan-2023 floods) with no ability to diversify geographically

Currently running below the Commerce Commission's own target regulatory return (5.53% actual vs ~7.82% targeted for PSE4 to date), showing execution/timing risk in translating capex into allowed returns

growth_drivers: Multi-billion dollar terminal integration and domestic jet terminal programme (targeted completion ~2029) adding 26% more domestic seat capacity and 44% more processing capacity
Airfield expansion (largest in company history, ~90% complete at H1-2026) adding resilience and six new remote aircraft stands
Property portfolio expansion - Manawa Bay outlet centre, Landing Business Park logistics developments (DHL Healthcare, IKEA), rent roll up 18% in FY25 with more pre-leased developments to come
New international air service connectivity (e.g., China Eastern's new Shanghai-Auckland-Buenos Aires route from Dec 2025) expanding transit and long-haul traffic
Recovery of international passenger volumes toward pre-COVID levels (92% of 2019 volumes as of FY25) as global aircraft fleet/engine constraints ease
2025 Master Plan provides a staged development blueprint to FY47, preserving an option for a second (northern) runway by FY38 without near-term capital commitment
Queenstown Airport equity stake provides indirect exposure to premium tourism catchment growth

business.description: Air New Zealand fleet/engine issues and, more recently, Middle East conflict-driven fuel cost spikes have caused airlines (Air NZ, Qantas, Emirates, Singapore Airlines) to cut capacity into/via Auckland, directly reducing passenger volumes and aeronautical revenue
Revenue is tied to discretionary travel; international volumes still below 2019 levels and domestic travel flat amid a subdued NZ economy
Seismic, volcanic and flood risk (2023 flood event still generating insurance recoveries/costs) with no geographic diversification

financial.description: FY26 capex guidance of $1.0-1.2 billion funded substantially by debt; total borrowings of ~$2.65bn at Dec-2025, with execution/cost-overrun risk on the multi-year terminal and airfield programme
Significant bond, AMTN, bank facility and commercial paper borrowings; interest expense remains a meaningful drag on profit despite recent easing
Actual aeronautical return of 5.53% for PSE4-to-date versus a targeted 7.82%, meaning capex is not yet being fully recovered in earnings

regulatory.description: Aeronautical charges set under a five-year Price Setting Event cycle (currently PSE4, FY23-FY27) subject to ComCom review; AIA discounted charges for the final two years of PSE4 following the March 2025 final report, capping upside

High Court dismissed the merits review appeal by Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch airports and NZ Airports Association against the Commerce Commission's revised WACC methodology; further consultation on conceded coding errors expected in 2026, with a risk regulatory settings become permanently less favourable

regulatory.risk: Potential legislative change to airport regulation
regulatory.description: MBIE reviewed airport regulation effectiveness in 2025 and has since indicated it is not pursuing legislative change, but political/airline lobbying for tighter regulation could resurface

macro.description: 2026 Middle East conflict has driven jet fuel prices sharply higher (from ~US$85-90/bbl to US$150-200/bbl), prompting airlines including Air New Zealand to raise fares and cut capacity by 3-5%, directly threatening AIA's FY26/FY27 passenger volumes and aeronautical revenue

macro.risk: NZ and global consumer/discretionary spending slowdown
macro.description: Subdued NZ domestic economy has kept domestic passenger and retail spend growth muted
As a highly leveraged, long-duration infrastructure asset, AIA's valuation and funding costs are sensitive to NZ and global interest rate movements

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global and NZ air travel continues a gradual post-COVID recovery (NZ international arrivals up ~9% for the year to March 2026), but the recovery is being disrupted in 2026 by a geopolitically-driven fuel price shock and constrained global aircraft/engine supply, creating near-term capacity headwinds even as underlying long-term demand for NZ tourism and trade connectivity remains intact
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high for aeronautical/retail/carpark revenue (tied to passenger and airline capacity cycles); low-to-moderate for the property segment (long leases, high occupancy provide ballast)
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - large regulated capital base and debt-funded, multi-year capex programme make both cost of funding and asset valuation sensitive to interest rate moves
key_input_costs: Construction/materials costs for the terminal and airfield capex programme
Jet fuel prices (indirect, via airline capacity decisions rather than AIA's own cost base)

recent_developments.event: H1 FY2026 interim results: revenue +4% to NZ$519.6m, EBITDAFI +6% to NZ$371.3m, net underlying profit +6% to NZ$157.1m, reported profit -5% to NZ$177.0m (lower investment property revaluation gain); passengers +2% to 9.64m; interim dividend 6.50cps
FY26 underlying profit guidance narrowed to $295-320 million (from $280-320 million at FY25 results) with capex guidance narrowed to $1.0-1.2 billion

Middle East conflict (from ~28 Feb 2026) drove jet fuel prices from ~US$85-90/bbl to US$150-200/bbl; Air New Zealand and other carriers (Qantas, Emirates, Singapore Airlines) raised fares and cut long-haul capacity 3-5%, a direct headwind to AIA passenger volumes into FY26/27; consensus analyst price target cut from NZ$9.00 to NZ$8.25 on this uncertainty

High Court dismissed the merits review appeal by Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch airports and the NZ Airports Association against the Commerce Commission's revised WACC/cost-of-capital methodology; further ComCom consultation on conceded coding errors expected during 2026
Finalised 2025 Master Plan released, setting a staged development blueprint to FY47 and preserving (but not committing to) a second northern runway option by FY38
China Eastern Airlines launched a new Shanghai-Auckland-Buenos Aires service via AKL, estimated to deliver ~$110m in annual economic benefit to New Zealand

Auckland Council/Auckland Future Fund completed sale of its remaining ~9.71% stake in Auckland Airport for at least $8.08/share (~$1.31bn), ending decades of council ownership, following a 2023 partial sale of 7% at $8.11/share

Commerce Commission's final PSE4 report confirmed AIA's infrastructure investment programme as reasonable; AIA responded by discounting airline charges for the final two years of PSE4, targeting a 7.82% return (down from an earlier higher target) but reporting only 5.53% actual return to date

FY2025 annual results: revenue +12% to $1,004.7m, EBITDAFI +14% to $701.1m, underlying profit +12% to $310.4m, reported profit +7,549% to $420.7m (prior year had a one-off tax charge); total dividend 13.25cps (71.9% payout of underlying profit)

items.notes: Narrowed from the $280-320 million range given at FY25 results (Aug 2025); reflects continued passenger recovery and network growth momentum, but issued before the Middle East fuel-price shock reached its peak

items.vs_prior: narrowed from $1,000-1,300 million range given at FY25 results
items.notes: Focused on the domestic jet terminal, airfield expansion and commercial/property developments

items.vs_prior: initial FY26 guidance given at FY25 results (Aug 2025)
items.notes: Given before the 2026 Middle East conflict/fuel spike and associated airline capacity cuts; actual outcomes likely to be pressured versus this base case

items.target: 70-90% of underlying net profit after tax
items.notes: Dividend reinvestment plan (DRP) offered at a 2.5% discount; H1 FY26 interim dividend declared at 6.50 cents per share, fully imputed

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Carrie Hurihanganui highlighted continued network growth (e.g., new China Eastern service) and infrastructure delivery progress, while flagging that ongoing airline seat capacity constraints, the geopolitical environment, and a live construction environment create uncertainty around the FY26 outlook. Guidance is explicitly described as cautious and subject to unforeseen events; the subsequent Middle East conflict and fuel price spike (from ~March 2026) represents a material downside risk to the passenger and earnings guidance issued in February 2026.

bull_case: Irreplaceable monopoly infrastructure asset serving New Zealand's largest city, with structural long-term growth in passenger and cargo volumes as international travel normalises above 2019 levels
Diversified, high-occupancy (99%) property and logistics portfolio provides a growing, more predictable earnings stream that partially offsets aeronautical cyclicality

Multi-billion dollar capex programme (domestic terminal, airfield expansion) directly expands capacity and, once commissioned, should convert into higher regulated and commercial revenue as the asset base grows

Commerce Commission's PSE4 final report validated the reasonableness of AIA's investment programme, reducing regulatory tail risk around cost recovery, and the High Court upheld the Commission's WACC framework, removing an overhang of uncertainty

Progressive, high-payout dividend policy (70-90% of underlying profit) with a DRP, appealing to income-focused NZX investors, alongside a strong A- credit rating supporting continued access to debt funding
bear_case: 2026 Middle East conflict and resulting fuel price spike is driving airline capacity cuts (Air NZ, Qantas, Emirates, Singapore Airlines all reducing schedules), directly threatening FY26/FY27 passenger volumes and aeronautical/retail revenue just as FY26 guidance was issued

Actual aeronautical returns (5.53%) remain well below the Commerce Commission's own targeted return (7.82%) for PSE4 to date, showing the enormous capex programme is not yet translating into commensurate earnings, with execution and cost-overrun risk through to terminal completion (~2029)

High leverage (~$2.65bn borrowings) funding a multi-year capex programme leaves the company exposed to interest rate and refinancing risk, and to the risk that regulatory settings (WACC methodology, future price-setting events) become less favourable after the unfavourable High Court ruling for airports
Consensus analyst price targets have already been cut (from NZ$9.00 to NZ$8.25) reflecting a more uncertain near-term outlook linked to the Middle East conflict continuing into FY2027

Single-site concentration risk (seismic, volcanic, flood) with no ability to diversify away from Auckland, and continued dependence on discretionary international tourism and a still-subdued NZ domestic economy
